title: Compartments
explain: A compartment logically separates a set of resources: its own namespace, access policy, quota and billing. Whether it also limits blast radius depends on a single question, is the isolation logical or physical? Two compartments with separate logical databases on one physical database still share its CPU, disk and fate.
model:
A compartment is a **logical boundary around resources**: who can touch what, and how much they may use (cloud account compartments, Kubernetes namespaces, per-team schemas).

The question that matters for blast radius: **what is shared underneath?**

| Isolation | Examples | What it gives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Logical | namespaces, schemas, IAM policies, quotas | access control, accounting, naming, smaller scope for human mistakes |
| Physical | separate hosts, clusters, networks, accounts | independent failure and independent performance |

User's own example: different compartments with different logical DBs that sit on **one physical DB**. One compartment's heavy query or the host dying still hurts the others.

Draw the boundary, then audit the shared layer: CPU, disk I/O, memory, connection limit, network, control plane. Close the gaps that matter:

1. Per-compartment resource caps (CPU, I/O, connections, query concurrency).
2. Dedicated clusters for critical compartments.
3. Promote a compartment to a [cell](#/sd/f/cell): a complete stack with no cross-access.

Compartments often implement [tenant isolation](#/sd/f/tenant-isolation).

details.q: Tenants A and B use separate Postgres schemas on one instance. A runs a heavy report and B slows down. Why?
details.a: Schemas are logical compartments that share the same CPU, I/O, memory and connection pool. The isolation is logical only, so contention crosses the boundary.

Each compartment on its own database cluster, or on dedicated hosts in a separate zone. Separate schemas in a shared cluster, or Kubernetes namespaces with quotas on the same nodes, are still logical or only partly isolated.

details.q: Eight compartments run on two physical database clusters, four each. One cluster dies. What share of traffic is lost?
details.a: Half, 50 percent. The blast radius follows the physical sharing, not the number of compartments.

details.q: What do logical compartments still give you when they share hardware?
details.a: Access control, quotas, cost attribution and a smaller scope for human mistakes (dropping the wrong table). They do not give hardware, performance or failure isolation.

details.q: How is a compartment different from a cell?
details.a: A cell is a complete, independently deployable stack with no cross-access, so isolation is by construction. A compartment is a boundary around some resources that may still share infrastructure.

details.q: How do you harden a logical compartment without going fully physical?
details.a: Enforce per-compartment limits on CPU, I/O, connections and query concurrency, add rate limits at the front, and move critical or noisy compartments to dedicated resources. This keeps most of the cost savings of sharing.

prompts.q: You are shown a diagram with several compartments. What do you ask first to estimate blast radius?
points: What is shared underneath the boundary
Hosts, databases, networks, connection pools, control plane
Which failure or load spike in one compartment can reach another
Logical separation limits access and quota, not shared-fate failures

prompts.q: Contrast logical and physical isolation with examples.
points: Physical: separate clusters, hosts, networks, accounts
Logical gives access control and accounting
Physical gives independent failure and performance

prompts.q: Compare a compartment and a cell and say when you would promote one to the other.
points: Cell is a full stack with no cross-access
Compartment is a boundary that may share infrastructure
Promote when a compartment is critical or noisy and shared fate is unacceptable
